Ephemeral state is anything no one outside the widget needs to read, and hoisting it into a shared store costs you free disposal, cheap rebuilds and screen independence while buying nothing.

### The test
- Does anything outside this widget read it? Must it survive the route being popped? Does the backend care? Three noes and it belongs in a `State` object.
- Ephemeral: the text mid-typing in a `TextEditingController`, the current `PageController` page, whether an `ExpansionTile` is open, whether a password field is masked.
- App state: the signed-in user, the cart, a cached feed, an unsent draft.

### What over-lifting costs
- The value now outlives the screen, so reopening it shows last week's search text until you write reset code that would not otherwise exist.
- Every keystroke goes through the store, so every listener that has not narrowed its read rebuilds too.
- Two live copies of the same screen — two tabs, a second pushed instance — fight over one field.
- Nothing disposes it when the route pops. The element tree used to do that for you.

### What promoting it later costs
- Almost nothing, and that is the point: lift the field, pass `value` plus `onChanged`, or read from the store. The compiler finds every call site for you.
- The reverse move is the expensive one, because first you have to prove no other reader exists.

Start local. Promote the moment a second reader appears or the value has to survive the route.

`final` freezes the reference, not the contents, so `sort()` reorders the one list every holder shares — including the state object your store still believes is unchanged.

### What actually breaks
- No notification fires. Nothing compared unequal, so `ValueNotifier`, Bloc and Riverpod all see no change and other widgets keep rendering the old order until something unrelated rebuilds them.
- Readers you never thought about get mutated data: a second screen showing the same list, a previous state kept for undo, a state you already emitted.
- Tests that captured a state and assert on it later see the mutated version, so a real bug passes.

### Why the compiler is quiet
- `final List<Item> items` only forbids reassigning the field. `List` itself is mutable, and `@immutable` is a lint about fields, not a deep guarantee.
- A `const []` default *is* unmodifiable and throws, which is why this bug usually hides until the first real page of data arrives.

### How to close it
- Never mutate what you were handed. Build a new list: `[...state.items]..sort(...)`.
- Return `List.unmodifiable(...)` from getters, or store an `UnmodifiableListView`, so a stray `add` throws at the call site instead of corrupting state silently.
- Change state only by emitting a new object holding a new list.

Treat everything reachable from a state object as read-only, one level deep or ten.

Either stop nesting — flatten the state and key the parts by id — or let a generator write the copies, because hand-written `copyWith` chains are exactly where fields go missing.

### Why hand-written chains rot
- Every level needs its own `copyWith` listing every field. Add a field, forget one level, and nothing complains: the omitted field quietly keeps `this.x`.
- The nullable trap rides along. `copyWith(middleName: null)` cannot clear anything, because the body reads `middleName ?? this.middleName` as "leave it alone". You need an explicit `clearMiddleName` flag or a sentinel value.
- A four-level rebuild allocates four objects to change one string, and every level's `==` has to be right or the change is swallowed.

### freezed
- `@freezed abstract class Profile with _$Profile` generates `==`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copyWith` and, with `@JsonSerializable`, the JSON too.
- Its `copyWith` uses a sentinel, so `copyWith(middleName: null)` genuinely clears the field.
- When a field's type is also freezed you get deep copy: `profile.copyWith.address(city: 'Almaty')`, and `?.` on the accessor when that field is nullable.
- The cost is `build_runner` in the loop and generated files in every diff.

### Or flatten
- Deep trees are usually missing normalization. Hold `Map<UserId, User>` and `Map<UserId, Address>` plus the ids, and one update touches one map entry.
- Nest state only as deep as the thing you replace atomically.

`List` has no value equality in Dart — `==` on a list is identity — so two lists built separately are never equal no matter what they contain, and your `==` is comparing references.

### What compares how
- `List`, `Map` and `Set`: identity by default. `[1, 2] == [1, 2]` is `false`.
- `const [1, 2] == const [1, 2]` is `true`, because identical const literals are canonicalised to one object. That is why the empty-default case looks fine and the bug only appears with real data.
- Records are structural: `(1, 'a') == (1, 'a')` is `true` — but a record holding a list falls back to that list's identity.
- `String`, `int`, `double`, `enum` and `DateTime` already compare by value.

### Fixing it
- `listEquals` / `mapEquals` from `package:flutter/foundation.dart`, or `DeepCollectionEquality().equals` from `package:collection` for nested structures.
- Hash the contents too: `Object.hash(Object.hashAll(items), loading)`. A right `==` with an identity-based `hashCode` silently breaks every `Set` and `Map` key.
- Equatable does both from `props`, and freezed's generated `==` uses `DeepCollectionEquality` for collection fields.

### The trap in the other direction
- Deep-comparing ten thousand rows on every emit is real work. If the list is rebuilt from one source, compare a cheap token instead — a revision int or the server's `updatedAt`.
- `==` and `hashCode` must always move together, and both must cover the same fields.

Nothing makes the three writes land together, so the tree can rebuild between them and render a combination that is not a legal state — page 4 of a filter that has one page.

### What over-splitting costs
- No atomic update. Three `notifyListeners()` calls are three chances to paint an inconsistent frame, and any widget reading two of them can see a torn pair.
- Invariants have nowhere to live. "the selection only contains visible items" is a rule about two objects, so it gets copy-pasted into whichever widget noticed the bug.
- Listeners that watch several notifiers run their expensive work once per notification instead of once per change.
- Tests must drive several objects to set up one scenario, and the setup no longer matches how the app moves.

### What one big object costs
- Every change produces a new object, so a listener that has not narrowed its read rebuilds on unrelated fields. That is a read-site problem — `context.select`, `BlocSelector`, `ref.watch(p.select(...))` — not a reason to split the model.

### Where the line goes
- One state object per unit of consistency: the fields that change together and are validated together.
- Split when lifetimes differ (a session outlives a screen) or write rates differ by orders of magnitude (a 60 Hz scroll offset next to a loaded page).
- Split on lifetime and write frequency, never on "these fields feel unrelated".

Anything computable from the other fields should not be a field — derive it in a getter and the object cannot disagree with itself.

### The three places, and how each drifts
1. **Computed in a getter.** `double get total => subtotal - discount;` cannot go stale, because there is nothing to keep up to date. It costs a recompute per read, which for arithmetic over a screenful of rows is nothing.
2. **Memoized in the holder.** Cached in the notifier or bloc and invalidated on write. Correct as long as every write path invalidates it — until someone adds a fourth mutation and forgets, which is this bug with more steps.
3. **Stored as a field.** The total is now a second source of truth for one fact. Every writer must remember to recompute it, and a wrong value gets serialized, restored and compared by `==` as if it were real.

### When storing is actually right
- The computation is genuinely expensive, the inputs change rarely, and it lives as a cache next to its inputs — keyed by the input, so a mismatch is detectable rather than invisible.
- The value is not derivable at all: a server-computed total with tax rules the client does not have. That is not derived state, it is fetched state, and it belongs in a field.

### Rules
- Getter first, measure before caching, and cache in the holder rather than in the state.
- Never serialize a derived value; a restored total that disagrees with the lines is invisible until someone checks the arithmetic.
- Keep derived values out of `props` and `==`. They are a function of the inputs, so they add nothing — and a stale one makes two different states compare equal.

Order the state by when the user decided, not by when the network answered: tag every intent with an id and discard any reply whose id is no longer the newest.

### Why "last write wins" is not the fix
- Last write wins describes which *response* arrives last, not which *tap* happened first. Save A (on) is slow, save B (off) is fast; B answers, then A answers, and the row goes back to on.
- `await` serializes nothing on its own. Two taps start two handler bodies that interleave at every await point, each holding its own captured copy of the old state.

### Three fixes, cheapest first
1. **Sequence token.** Keep an `int _requestId` on the holder, increment it per intent, capture it locally, and after the await return early if `id != _requestId`. Four lines, no dependency, works under any state library.
2. **Serialize the writes.** Funnel them so only one is ever in flight — that is exactly what bloc's `sequential()`, `droppable()` and `restartable()` transformers do for events.
3. **Cancel the loser.** Dio's `CancelToken` or closing the `http.Client`. Keep the id check anyway, because cancellation itself races the response.

### Details that bite
- Check `isClosed` or `mounted` after every await too; the screen may already be gone.
- Debounce the intent rather than racing requests: a toggle flipped twice ends where it started, so send only the settled value after ~300 ms.
- Make the write idempotent or versioned server-side — `If-Match`, or an `updatedAt` precondition — so a late request cannot overwrite newer data even when it does arrive.

Apply the change locally at once, keep the value you replaced inside the state next to the pending row, and put it back — visibly — when the server refuses.

### The shape
- Each row carries its own sync status, not one screen-level `isSaving` flag; with two rows in flight a single boolean cannot say which one failed.
- On tap: write the new value, mark the row pending, and store the previous value in the state rather than in a local variable, so a rebuild or a second tap cannot lose the rollback.
- On success: clear the pending mark and drop the saved value.
- On failure: restore the saved value, mark it failed, and surface the message as a one-shot effect — a stream or a callback — never as a permanent field that replays on every rebuild.

### What the row shows while pending
- The new value, immediately. That is the entire point; do not replace the content with a spinner. At most add a quiet "not synced" affordance, and keep the control tappable when the action is idempotent.

### Traps
- Rolling back to a stale value. Between the tap and the failure the server may have changed the row; restore what you replaced, then reconcile on the next fetch.
- Server-generated data cannot be optimistic. Insert with a temporary local id, swap it when the response lands, and update anything holding the temp id.
- Do not make a delete optimistic unless you can fully rebuild the row locally.

Optimistic UI is a promise you must be able to take back. If you cannot compute the rollback, do not make the promise.

Put the paging position in the state as data — the cursor the next page continues from — and make every response prove it still belongs to the state it lands in.

### The shape
- `items`, `nextCursor` (null means the end), `isLoadingMore`, `isRefreshing`. There is no `hasMore` field: it is `nextCursor != null`, so the two can never disagree.
- A load-more request remembers the cursor it was built from. When the response arrives, append only if `state.nextCursor` is still that cursor. If it is not, a refresh reset the list underneath it and the page is stale — drop it.
- Refresh replaces `items` and `nextCursor` in a single write instead of clearing and then loading, so the list never blinks empty on the way through.

### Why flags alone fail
- `page`, `hasMore`, `isLoading`, `isRefreshing` as four independent fields give sixteen combinations of which about five are legal, and none of them tells a late response that it is late.
- An `int page` counter is worse than a cursor even without a race: after a refresh, page three of the old list is page two of the new one, so offset paging repeats or skips rows.
- Guard re-entrancy on `isLoadingMore`, or one flick of the thumb fires the same page four times.

### Details that bite
- De-duplicate by stable id when appending. An overlapping row from a live feed is legitimate, not a bug.
- "Loaded and empty" and "not loaded yet" must be distinguishable — empty `items` plus a null cursor plus no request in flight is the empty state, and it renders differently from the first load.

Rule of thumb: if two fields in a state can contradict each other, one of them should have been a getter.

Because each of those screens took its own copy of the name, and a copy has no way to hear about an edit — the value needs exactly one owner that every reader watches.

### Single source of truth
- The repository, or one store above the routes, owns the profile and exposes it as something listenable: a `Stream`, a `ValueNotifier`, a provider. The edit writes once, all three readers rebuild.
- Screens keep no `String _name` field. The only local copy that is allowed is a text controller while the user is typing, and that is a draft, not the value.
- The staleness bug this shape still creates: a screen that reads once into local state in `initState` is invisible from the outside and drifts forever. Same bug, smaller box.

### Invalidation events
- The editor publishes `ProfileChanged(id)` and listeners refetch. You need this when the data is too large to hold in memory, or lives in a database that something else also writes.
- Its staleness bug: whoever was not listening at the instant the event fired — disposed, backgrounded, not yet built — never learns. Events are point-in-time; state is not. You also get N refetches for one edit.
- The fix is to make the store the listener rather than the screens. The event invalidates a cache, the cache re-emits, and the screens are back to watching one value.

### Choosing
- Small, hot values — profile, cart, feature flags — one owner holding the value.
- Large or externally written data — one owner holding a query, invalidated by events, re-emitting the result.

Either way there is exactly one owner. Two owners of the same value is not a caching strategy, it is the bug you are debugging.

In one draft object owned by the flow — not by any single step, and not by the domain model it will eventually become.

### The draft is its own type
- `SignupDraft` has nullable, unvalidated fields; `Signup`, the thing you actually send, has non-nullable validated ones. Converting one to the other is a single function that either hands back a real object or tells you what is missing.
- That split is what keeps "half a user" out of the repository. If the steps wrote into the domain model directly, every field downstream would have to stay nullable forever to accommodate the wizard.
- Per-step validity is derived from the draft, never stored as its own flag, or the Next button and the data eventually disagree.

### Ownership and lifetime
- The holder is created by the route that opens the flow and disposed when that route leaves, so every step reads and writes the same instance and "discard" is just leaving. There is nothing to reset by hand.
- Do not hang it off a singleton or the app scope. The second run of the flow then opens pre-filled with the abandoned first one — a support ticket rather than a crash, which is worse.
- Commit is one write at the end: build the domain object, call the repository once, clear the draft only after it succeeds. Writing each step to the server as you go turns every abandonment into an orphaned record you now have to clean up.

### Surviving a restart
- Persisting the draft is optional and decided per flow. If you do it, serialize the draft type rather than widget state, version the payload, and delete it the moment the commit succeeds.
- Ask what a restored form means. Bringing back a half-typed signup is friendly; bringing back a payment flow that may already have been charged is not.

A draft is data the user has not agreed to yet, so it never touches the model other screens read.

Restore where the user was and what they typed, re-fetch everything the server owns, and never restore credentials or anything that claims an action already happened.

### The three mechanisms
- **Framework restoration** — `restorationScopeId` on `MaterialApp` plus `RestorationMixin` and `RestorableProperty` in a `State`. The OS hands the app back a bucket of small values, so the route stack and text fields return without your storage layer being involved. Small, UI-shaped values only.
- **Hydrating from storage** — you write state to disk on change and read it at launch. Works for anything, costs an IO write per change, and hands you the versioning problem: that blob was written by an older build of the app.
- **Re-fetching** — restore the route and the identifiers, then load again from the network. Correct by construction, costs a spinner. It is the right default for anything the server owns.

### What must not come back
- Tokens, decrypted data, a biometric unlock. A restored `Authenticated` state outlives the token behind it and shows a signed-in shell that 401s on the first tap; re-derive the session from the refresh token instead.
- One-shot effects: a queued snackbar, a pending navigation, "payment in progress". Re-entering a payment you cannot prove finished is worse than starting over — ask the server for the order's status.
- Anything derived. Recompute it from what you did restore, or the two drift apart.

### The trap
This is not a rebuild — the isolate is new. `initState` runs from scratch, every singleton is freshly constructed, and anything held only in a static is null. Code that survives a rotation can still be broken here.

Reproduce it deliberately: Android's "Don't keep activities" developer option, or `adb shell am kill <package>` while the app is backgrounded. Pressing Back proves nothing, because that tears the app down for real.

Replace the booleans with a closed set of named states plus one total transition function, so the illegal combination has no way to be spelled.

### Making illegal states unrepresentable
- Four independent booleans are sixteen combinations; the flow has five. The other eleven are bugs waiting for the right ordering of two callbacks.
- A `sealed` family — `Idle`, `Submitting`, `AwaitingConfirmation(paymentId)`, `Paid(receipt)`, `Failed(reason)` — collapses them to exactly those five, and each carries only the data that state actually has. `Paid` holds a receipt, so no branch can render a receipt screen without one, and `Idle` has no `paymentId` field left over to go stale.
- Dart's exhaustive `switch` then makes the UI total: add a state later and every switch that ignores it stops compiling.

### The transition function
- `CheckoutState next(CheckoutState, CheckoutEvent)` — pure, synchronous, no IO. Effects are decided by the caller from what changed rather than performed inside.
- Every pair of state and event has an answer, and the answer for an illegal pair is "stay put", not throw. A `Confirmed` arriving twice — a retry, a duplicate push, a double tap — has to be idempotent, because the network guarantees it will happen.
- Async work re-enters as an event: `SubmitSucceeded`, `SubmitFailed`. That is what stops a slow response from writing into a flow the user already cancelled; the transition simply ignores it in `Idle`.

### What the table buys you
- The transition table is the spec and it is test data. One parameterised test over every state times every event pins the whole machine in a screenful, including the pairs nobody thought about.
- The diagram in the ticket and the code stop drifting, because a product manager can read the table.
- No widget tree, no fakes, no clock — those tests run in microseconds.

The state holder outlived the screen that owned it: it was created above the route — a singleton, or a provider at app scope — so popping disposed the widgets and nothing else.

### Where a holder belongs
- Its scope is the shortest lifetime shared by everyone who reads it. Only this screen reads those filters, so the holder is created by the route and dies with it.
- Screen-scoped: filters, selections, a form draft, a pager. Session-scoped: the signed-in user, the cart, feed caches — these must outlive routes but must not outlive sign-out. App-scoped: theme, locale, connectivity, the HTTP client.
- Whoever creates a holder disposes it. A holder created by a route and disposed by nobody is exactly this bug.

### How a leaked holder shows up
- Stale UI, as in the question: the second visit starts in the first visit's state and reads like a caching bug rather than a lifetime bug.
- A late write. The pending future from visit one still holds a live reference and overwrites what visit two just loaded, so the screen "flickers back" a second later.
- Growth. Its subscriptions and listeners are still registered, so every visit adds another one and the callback runs N times.
- The mirror-image mistake — a callback writing to a holder that *is* disposed — throws instead. Guard the write after an await; do not delete the disposal to make the error go away.

### Keeping state on purpose
- Deliberate survival is fine: a list you want back instantly on Back is kept by hoisting the holder one scope up. Write down why, because the next reader cannot tell "cached" from "leaked" by looking.
- At sign-out, recreate the session scope instead of calling `clear()` on each store. A per-store cleanup list is one merge away from being incomplete; disposing a scope cannot forget.

Rule of thumb: name the event that should erase this state — screen popped, user signed out, app killed. That event is the scope.

With a version number stored next to the payload, a chain of small migrations from every old shape to the current one, and a load path where an unreadable blob is discarded rather than fatal.

### The envelope
- Persist `{"v": 3, "data": {...}}`, never a bare object. Without the number you are guessing the shape from its keys, and that guess gets worse every release.
- Migrations are pure `Map -> Map` functions applied in order. Users skip versions — someone updates from a build eleven months old — so the chain must run from any starting point, not only from the previous one.
- Additive changes need no migration if the reader supplies defaults for missing keys. Renames, splits and type changes do.
- Persist the domain model, not the UI state class. That class grows an `isRefreshing` flag every sprint and none of that belongs on disk.

### The load path
1. Read the blob. Missing means a first launch: return the initial state, and do not log it as an error.
2. Parse the envelope. If `v` is greater than the current version, the user rolled back or restored a backup from a newer install — discard it, do not attempt it.
3. Run the migration chain from `v` to current, then decode.
4. On any throw: log with the version, delete the key, return the initial state.

### Why step 4 is the whole answer
- Delete before you return. If the bad blob stays on disk the next launch reads it again, and you have shipped a crash loop that no restart fixes and no user escapes without reinstalling.
- Wrap the migrations in the same try as the decode. A migration written against a shape you assumed will eventually meet one you did not.
- Keep a fixture per shipped version in the test suite and assert each one loads into the current model. The old writer no longer exists in the codebase, so fixtures are the only proof the chain still works.
- Never version by app version. A schema version increments only when the shape changes.

Split the part that decides from the part that performs: a pure transition you can call directly, with time, IO and randomness injected rather than reached for.

### Make the transition pure
- `State next(State, Event)` takes a state and an input and returns a state. No `await`, no repository, no `DateTime.now()`. A test is then one line — give it a state, give it an event, compare the result.
- Async work lives outside as an effect that eventually feeds an event back in: `Loaded(items)`, `Failed(error)`. What you are testing is the transition table, not the network.
- Value equality on the state class is what makes `expect(next(s, e), expected)` readable. Without `==` you assert field by field and soon stop bothering.

### Assert the sequence, not the final value
- `expectLater(store.stream, emitsInOrder([isA<Loading>(), isA<Ready>()]))`. A test that checks only the end state passes on a flow that flashed an error frame on the way — which is the bug users actually report.
- To pin the in-flight state, hand the fake repository a `Completer` and complete it by hand. You now own the moment the response lands, so "two taps while the first is loading" is a deterministic test instead of a race.
- Assert on emissions, not on how many times a listener fired. A holder that emits an equal state twice is a separate bug with a separate test.

### Inject everything non-deterministic
- Clocks: `package:clock`'s `clock.now()` under `withClock`, or a `DateTime Function()` constructor parameter. A state carrying `DateTime.now()` is unequal to itself a millisecond later, and no expected value can be written down.
- Ids and randomness: pass in the generator. A `Uuid().v4()` called inside the transition makes the result unassertable for the same reason.
- Timers: never sleep. `fakeAsync` gives you virtual time, so a debounce or a five-minute backoff runs in microseconds.

Keep widget tests for what only a tree can prove: that a given state renders the right pixels.
